title: Europe’s Hera Spacecraft Begins Detailed Survey of NASA‑Rammed Asteroid After 2022 Test
body:
A European probe has now begun its first close‑up survey of the binary asteroid system Didymos, the very target that NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) deliberately struck in September 2022. The ESA‑operated Hera spacecraft, launched in October 2023, is orbiting the pair at distances as short as 15 miles (24 kilometres) and will spend the coming months mapping the impact crater, measuring the altered orbit and gathering data that could shape the future of planetary‑defence strategies.

The DART mission, a joint effort between NASA and several international partners, was the first ever kinetic‑impact test of an asteroid‑deflection technique. By crashing a 610‑kilogram spacecraft into Didymos’s small moonlet, Dimorphos, at roughly 6 km s⁻¹, DART succeeded in shifting the moon’s orbital period by about 33 minutes – a clear demonstration that a high‑speed impact can change an asteroid’s trajectory. Hera’s arrival marks the next logical step: a detailed forensic examination of the aftermath, something that could not be achieved from Earth‑based telescopes alone.

Hera’s mission profile is ambitious. After a series of deep‑space maneuvers, the spacecraft entered a highly elliptical orbit around Didymos on 23 October, gradually lowering its periapsis to bring it within a few dozen kilometres of Dimorphos. Onboard instruments—including a high‑resolution camera, a laser altimeter, a thermal infrared spectrometer and a low‑frequency radar—will produce three‑dimensional maps of the impact site, assess the distribution of ejecta, and probe the internal structure of both bodies. By comparing pre‑impact models with the post‑impact reality, scientists hope to refine the physics of momentum transfer, a key variable in calculating how much force an impact can impart on a potentially hazardous asteroid.

The data will also inform the European Union’s upcoming Hera‑L mission concept, which envisions a fleet of small satellites that could be dispatched to multiple near‑Earth objects in the coming decade. “We are moving from a proof‑of‑concept to a quantitative understanding of how kinetic impacts work,” said Dr. Luca D’Angelo, ESA’s mission manager for Hera, during a briefing at the agency’s headquarters in Paris. “The measurements we obtain will be the benchmark for any future deflection effort, whether it involves a kinetic impactor, a gravity tractor or a more exotic approach.”

Beyond planetary defence, the mission offers a rare glimpse into the composition and evolution of binary asteroids, which make up a significant fraction of near‑Earth objects. Didymos and Dimorphos are thought to be rubble‑pile bodies—aggregates of rock and dust held together by their own weak gravity. Understanding how such loosely bound structures respond to high‑energy collisions could also shed light on the early solar system, when planetesimals coalesced and fragmented. Moreover, the mission’s radar and spectrometer data may reveal the presence of water‑bearing minerals, an aspect of interest for future resource‑utilisation initiatives.

As Hera continues its systematic survey, the international community watches closely. The United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) has highlighted the DART‑Hera collaboration as a model for multinational cooperation in safeguarding Earth from cosmic threats. While the immediate focus is scientific, the broader implication is clear: humanity now possesses both the technology to test an asteroid‑deflection technique and the means to evaluate its effectiveness in situ. The lessons learned will feed directly into contingency planning for any asteroid whose trajectory poses a genuine impact risk in the next century.

Looking ahead, the next phase of the mission will involve a series of low‑altitude passes that could bring Hera within a few kilometres of Dimorphos, allowing the spacecraft to capture unprecedented detail of the crater and the surrounding debris field. Those observations will be crucial for calibrating computer models that predict how different asteroid types would react to an impact. With the data set expected to be released gradually over the next two years, the scientific and engineering communities will have a robust foundation to design the next generation of planetary‑defence missions, ensuring that the brief success of DART is not a one‑off experiment but the beginning of a reliable, globally coordinated shield against celestial hazards.
